chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Abu Basir asked him, 'How much is the qamah (height of the shadow)?' He said, 'A cubit. Indeed, the qamah of the saddle of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was a cubit.' The third [point] is that the shadow of the standing person, by which the time of zawal (solar noon) is determined, varies according to the variation of times. Sometimes the shadow ends on him in the palaces, so that nothing remains between him and the base of the erected pole more than a foot. Sometimes it ends at a point that is a cubit between him and it. Sometimes its amount is equal to the height of the erected pole. When the shadow returns to increase and adds as much as it had previously reached from the limit, then the time has entered, whether it was a foot, a cubit, or equal to the body of the erected pole. Therefore, the consideration is by the shadow in all states, not by the body of the erected pole, and that which indicates this meaning.

key_terms.الزَّوَالُ: Solar noon, the moment the sun reaches its highest point in the sky.
key_terms.الْعَمُودِ الْمَنْصُوبِ: The erected pole, used as a reference for shadow measurement.
key_terms.الْقَامَةُ: The height or length, specifically referring to the length of the shadow at its minimum.
key_terms.ذِرَاعٌ: A cubit, a traditional unit of measurement.

ai.seo_question: How is the start time of Dhuhr prayer determined using shadow measurement?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the precise astronomical criterion for Dhuhr prayer onset, distinguishing between the absolute zenith (Qibla shadow disappearance) and the start of the prayer time (shadow expansion). It highlights the scholarly consensus that the measurement of shadow increase is relative to the specific minimum length observed at that location and time, rather than a fixed standard, ensuring accurate prayer timing across varying latitudes and seasons. This practical jurisprudence underscores the Shia emphasis on observable natural signs as divinely ordained markers for worship.
